name: Public exposure auditor — three audits in one turn, correlated into a chain
_why: Pins the read-only four-phase shape end to end: TRIAGE decides the work,
GATHER asks for all three audits in ONE turn and parks, HYPOTHESIZE reasons
with no tools at all, and REPORT ships with every factual line cited.
The single-turn fan-out is the behaviour worth protecting. The three audits
are independent, so asking for them one at a time triples the wall-clock of
a run for no extra information — and a prompt edit that makes the model
serialise them would otherwise be invisible until someone timed a real run.
It also pins that the run FINISHes with no uncited claims: the report below
is written the way the persona asks for, and if the evidence heuristic ever
starts flagging an honest 'could not read' caveat, this fails.

tools.name: workflow_31
tools.description: Lists every S3 bucket in the account with its public access block, ACL grants, bucket-policy public status, default encryption and versioning. Read-only.

tools.name: workflow_32
tools.description: Finds every security-group rule open to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 in one region, and reports what is actually attached behind each one. Read-only.

tools.name: workflow_33
tools.description: Reads the account's IAM credential report and reports access-key age, last use, MFA status and console access per principal. Read-only.

event.input: Audit the eu-west-1 account for anything reachable from the internet.

value.restated: Find what in the eu-west-1 account is reachable from the internet, and what an attacker could do once there.
observations_needed: Which buckets are public, and whether a block or a policy makes them so
Which security-group rules are open to the world, and what is attached behind them
Which principals hold stale or unused credentials

script.text: All three audits returned. I have what I need.

findings.summary: customer-invoices is readable by the internet: its bucket policy grants public access and no public access block is in force to override it.
sg-0f1e2d3c4b5a69780 opens SSH to the whole internet and has a live internet-facing load balancer attached.
deploy-bot holds an access key 412 days old that has never been used — the cheapest item here to remove, because nothing depends on it.
sg-0aaabbbccc111222 opens MySQL to the world but is attached to nothing, so it is housekeeping rather than an exposure.

script.text:
**One bucket is readable by the internet, and the account holds a credential that would let an attacker keep moving.**

- `customer-invoices` is public: its bucket policy grants public access, and its public access block is ABSENT so nothing overrides that grant [e:501].
- Security group `sg-0f1e2d3c4b5a69780` opens SSH to the whole internet and has an internet-facing load balancer attached [e:502].
- The IAM user `deploy-bot` holds an access key 412 days old that has never been used [e:503].

The chain that matters: the open SSH rule is a way in, and `deploy-bot`'s unused key is a credential that would survive a password reset.

Do first:

- Remove `deploy-bot`'s access key. Nothing has ever called it, so removing it breaks nothing.
- Put the public access block back on `customer-invoices`, then take the public statement out of its bucket policy. Both are needed; either alone leaves the grant in place.

Lower priority: `sg-0aaabbbccc111222` opens MySQL to the world but is attached to nothing, so it is tidying rather than exposure [e:502].

Not checked: the encryption configuration on one bucket could not be read, so its encryption state is unknown.
